solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle 1748 Madras exchange
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students recall 'Clive' as the defining English figure of the Carnatic Wars and may assume he negotiated the First War's settlement, when in fact the outcome was determined entirely by the European treaty.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options suggesting Madras was retained by England after a military victory — no such battlefield outcome decided this; the First Carnatic War ended by European treaty.
Eliminate any option naming a treaty signed on Indian soil — the settlement was concluded at Aix-la-Chapelle in Europe.
Identify that Madras was exchanged for Louisbourg in Canada, confirming option b as the correct pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The classic trap here is assuming that outcomes of wars fought in India were settled in India. The First Carnatic War ended not through any military decision on Indian soil but through the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) in Europe, which resolved the War of Austrian Succession. Under this treaty, Madras was returned to England in exchange for Louisbourg in Canada — two entirely different continents. Students who focus only on the Indian theatre miss this transatlantic dimension entirely.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Carnatic War (1746–1748) was an extension of the War of Austrian Succession in Europe. France captured Madras in 1746 under Dupleix after defeating the English naval commander Peyton. However, its resolution had nothing to do with Indian battlefield outcomes.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Madras was not retained by France; it was returned to England under the treaty.
• Option (b): Correct. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) ended the War of Austrian Succession. Under its terms, Madras was restored to England in exchange for Louisbourg, a French fortress in Canada — demonstrating that India was merely one theatre of a global rivalry.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Robert Clive's decisive contributions came in the Second Carnatic War (Arcot, 1751), not in settling the First.
• Option (d): Incorrect. No separate treaty was signed at Pondicherry to end the First Carnatic War; that treaty came later in 1754.

Value Addition:
• Battle of St. Thome (1746): French forces under Paradis defeated Nawab Anwaruddin's much larger army — early proof of European tactical superiority.
• The exchange of Madras for Louisbourg illustrates how colonial possessions were treated as bargaining chips in European diplomacy.
• La Bourdonnais, not Dupleix, commanded the naval operation that captured Madras; the two subsequently clashed over the city's fate.

solution.concept_anchor: Dupleix strategy embryonic subsidiary alliance origins

statement_analysis.statement: Dupleix was the first European to systematically intervene in Indian succession disputes to secure territorial and financial concessions from the victorious claimant.
statement_analysis.reason: Dupleix pioneered the practice of backing rival claimants (Chanda Sahib in Carnatic, Muzaffar Jung in Hyderabad) in exchange for territory and revenue — a template for all subsequent European intervention.

statement_analysis.statement: The policy later formalised as 'Subsidiary Alliance' was conceived and given its definitive structure by Dupleix during the Carnatic Wars.
statement_analysis.reason: Dupleix practised only an embryonic, informal version of this policy; the Subsidiary Alliance was formally systematised and given institutional shape by Lord Wellesley from 1798 onwards.

statement_analysis.statement: The French Compagnie des Indes recalled Dupleix partly because his territorial ambitions imposed financial costs that the state-controlled company could not sustain.
statement_analysis.reason: The French Compagnie, dependent on the royal treasury and prioritising trade over empire, recalled Dupleix in 1754 precisely because his interventionist strategy generated mounting expenditure without proportionate commercial returns.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d ('1 and 2 and 3') is deceptive because Statement 2 sounds plausible to a student who knows Dupleix 'originated' subsidiary alliance thinking, leading them to mark all three correct without distinguishing between conceptual origin and formal systematisation.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Dupleix's backing of Chanda Sahib and Muzaffar Jung in exchange for concessions is textbook — Statement 1 is correct.
Scrutinise Statement 2: Wellesley formally systematised Subsidiary Alliance from 1798; Dupleix's version was embryonic and informal, so 'definitive structure' in Statement 2 makes it incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: The French Compagnie was state-controlled and financially strained — recall of Dupleix for financial reasons is well-established — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct, pointing to option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the designed trap. Students who have read that Dupleix 'originated' the idea of subsidiary alliance often extend this to mean he also gave it a definitive structure. The distinction is crucial: Dupleix practised an informal, ad hoc version; Wellesley formalised it as a deliberate imperial instrument from 1798. UPSC frequently tests this attribution distinction — crediting Dupleix with the concept while correctly crediting Wellesley with the formalisation.
solution.final_explanation:
Dupleix's strategy during the Carnatic Wars marked a turning point in European engagement with Indian politics — moving from purely commercial dealings to deliberate political interference.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Dupleix systematically backed rival succession claimants (Chanda Sahib in Carnatic, Muzaffar Jung in Hyderabad) in exchange for territory and revenue, pioneering the model of extracting concessions through military support.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: While Dupleix practised the underlying logic, the Subsidiary Alliance as a formal, institutionalised system was the creation of Lord Wellesley (from 1798). Attributing the 'definitive structure' to Dupleix overstates his contribution.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The French Compagnie des Indes, being state-controlled and financially constrained, prioritised commerce over territorial expansion. Dupleix's wars drained resources without commercial payoff, prompting his recall in 1754.

Value Addition:
• Dupleix's recall was a strategic gift to the English — no French leader of comparable political vision succeeded him in India.
• Wellesley used Subsidiary Alliance to subordinate Hyderabad (1798), Mysore (1799), and the Marathas (1802) — all theatres Dupleix had earlier contested.
• The contrast between the English EIC (private, profit-driven) and the French Compagnie (state-controlled, treasury-dependent) is a recurring UPSC analytical theme.

solution.concept_anchor: Siege of Arcot 1751 Clive strategic logic

statement_analysis.statement: Robert Clive captured Arcot with approximately 200 soldiers, aiming to relieve the pressure on Muhammad Ali at Trichinopoly by threatening the political capital of Carnatic.
statement_analysis.reason: Clive's force of around 200 soldiers captured Arcot with the precise strategic intent of diverting Chanda Sahib's forces away from Trichinopoly — an indirect relief operation.

statement_analysis.statement: The defence of Arcot lasted approximately 53 days, during which Clive's forces repelled an attacking army numbering around 10,000 before being relieved by a Maratha contingent.
statement_analysis.reason: The 53-day defence against a force of approximately 10,000 is historically documented; Morari Rao's Marathas did provide support that aided the English position.

statement_analysis.statement: Arcot was primarily significant as an open-field battle that demonstrated the superiority of English infantry tactics over French-trained Indian forces.
statement_analysis.reason: Arcot was a siege and defence operation, not an open-field engagement; moreover, the opposing forces were primarily Chanda Sahib's troops supported by French allies, and the significance was psychological and strategic rather than a demonstration of infantry formation superiority.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b ('2 only') tempts students who know Statement 3 is wrong but second-guess the Maratha detail in Statement 2, as Maratha involvement is less frequently emphasised.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Clive's ~200-strong capture of Arcot to divert Chanda Sahib from Trichinopoly is a well-established fact — Statement 1 is correct.
Confirm Statement 2: The 53-day defence and Maratha support (Morari Rao) are historically documented — Statement 2 is correct.
Identify Statement 3 as incorrect: Arcot was a siege and defence, not an open-field battle, and the significance was strategic/psychological, not a demonstration of infantry formation superiority.
Since only Statement 3 is NOT correct, the answer is option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits a common conflation between the significance of Arcot and open-field engagements like Plassey or Wandiwash. Students who have a general impression that 'Clive won battles' may not pause to distinguish between a siege/defence operation and an open-field engagement. The further addition of 'French-trained Indian forces' in Statement 3 sounds plausible — Chanda Sahib did have French support — but the description of Arcot as primarily an infantry-tactics demonstration is factually wrong.
solution.final_explanation:
The Siege of Arcot (1751) is one of the most strategically inventive operations of the Carnatic Wars, but it is frequently mischaracterised.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Clive captured Arcot (capital of the Carnatic Nawab) with roughly 200 soldiers specifically to compel Chanda Sahib to divert forces from Trichinopoly — an indirect relief of the main theatre.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Clive then defended Arcot for 53 days against approximately 10,000 attackers. Maratha forces under Morari Rao provided timely support, reflecting how English success depended on Indian coalitions.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Arcot was fundamentally a siege and defence operation, not an open-field engagement. Its significance was primarily psychological (establishing English credibility as a political-military actor) and strategic (forcing Chanda Sahib to split his forces), not a demonstration of infantry formation superiority.

Value Addition:
• Arcot marked the English EIC's transition from trading company to political-military actor in southern India.
• Chanda Sahib was eventually captured and executed by Tanjore forces in 1752 — the direct consequence of Clive's Arcot strategy paying off.
• Clive's methods at Arcot — bold offensive action, psychological warfare, coalition-building — became the template he later applied at Plassey (1757).

solution.concept_anchor: Battle of Wandiwash 1760 commanders and significance

statement_analysis.statement: The Battle of Wandiwash was fought on January 22, 1760.
statement_analysis.reason: This date is historically documented and widely cited as the date of the decisive engagement.

statement_analysis.statement: The English forces at Wandiwash were commanded by Sir Eyre Coote, who defeated the French army led by Count de Lally.
statement_analysis.reason: Sir Eyre Coote commanded the victorious English force; Count de Lally commanded the French — this pairing is accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: Marquis de Bussy was killed during the Battle of Wandiwash, removing the most capable French commander from the Indian theatre.
statement_analysis.reason: Bussy was captured, not killed, at Wandiwash — his capture was still a decisive blow to French prospects, but stating he was killed is factually wrong.

statement_analysis.statement: Wandiwash is best compared to the Battle of Plassey (1757) because both battles ended the political power of the same regional power — the Nawabs of Carnatic.
statement_analysis.reason: Plassey (1757) ended the Nawab of Bengal's power, not the Carnatic Nawab's; Wandiwash ended French offensive capacity in India. These are different theatres and different consequences.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c ('Only three') tempts students who know Bussy was 'removed' at Wandiwash and conflate capture with death, making three pairs seem correct.
elimination_logic: Confirm pair 1: January 22, 1760 is the recorded date of Wandiwash — correct.
Confirm pair 2: Eyre Coote vs Lally is the accurate commander pairing — correct.
Reject pair 3: Bussy was captured, not killed, at Wandiwash — incorrect.

Reject pair 4: Plassey ended the Nawab of Bengal's power; Wandiwash ended French power — the comparison in Statement 4 conflates two different theatres, making it incorrect. Only two pairs are correct, pointing to option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two traps operate simultaneously. First, 'killed' vs 'captured' for Bussy — students who know Bussy was 'removed' at Wandiwash may not recall the precise manner. Second, Statement 4 deliberately conflates Plassey and Wandiwash by suggesting both affected Carnatic Nawabs — a geographic-swap trap, since Plassey was in Bengal, not Carnatic.
solution.final_explanation:
The Battle of Wandiwash (1760) was the decisive engagement that permanently destroyed French offensive military capability in India.

• Pair 1 — Correct: January 22, 1760 is the established date of the battle.
• Pair 2 — Correct: Sir Eyre Coote commanded English forces; Count de Lally led the French — both identifications are accurate.
• Pair 3 — Incorrect: Marquis de Bussy was captured at Wandiwash, not killed. His capture was still strategically catastrophic for France — he was their most experienced Indian-theatre commander — but the statement's use of 'killed' makes it factually wrong.
• Pair 4 — Incorrect: Plassey (1757) ended the political power of the Nawab of Bengal (Siraj-ud-Daulah), not the Carnatic Nawab. Wandiwash ended French offensive capacity in India. These are different theatres, different opponents, and different consequences.

Value Addition:
• Lally had recalled Bussy from Hyderabad to fight at Wandiwash — a double strategic error that weakened both the Deccan and the battlefield simultaneously.
• Fall of Pondicherry followed in 1761 — the English razed it to prevent its future use as a base.
• Bussy's earlier period in Hyderabad (1751–58) was the high point of French political influence in the Deccan.

solution.concept_anchor: French commanders events territorial holdings India
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because it correctly places Bussy in Hyderabad but swaps La Bourdonnais's role, tempting students who know the Bussy-Hyderabad connection but are less precise about the naval dimension.
elimination_logic: A (Marquis de Bussy) is unambiguously linked to Hyderabad — he controlled Nizam Salabat Jung's court 1751–1758 — so A matches 3.
B (La Bourdonnais) commanded the French naval force that captured Madras in 1746 — B matches 1.
C (Count de Lally) arrived in 1758 and was defeated at Wandiwash in 1760 — C matches 4.
D (Northern Circars) were the coastal Andhra territories ceded to France during Bussy's Hyderabad period — D matches 2. This gives A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2, which is option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary trap is the Bussy–Northern Circars linkage. Students may know Bussy was in Hyderabad but confuse who actually held the Northern Circars — these coastal Andhra territories were ceded to France as a result of Bussy's influence over the Nizam, not a separate military conquest. Option b swaps La Bourdonnais and Lally, exploiting the fact that both are French commanders associated with naval/military operations in roughly the same period.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precise knowledge of French personnel, events, and territorial holdings during the Carnatic Wars.

Correct pairings:
• A (Marquis de Bussy) — 3 (Wielded dominant influence over Nizam Salabat Jung in Hyderabad, 1751–58): Bussy was France's most effective political operator, essentially controlling Deccan politics from the Nizam's court for seven years.
• B (La Bourdonnais) — 1 (French naval commander who captured Madras in 1746): La Bourdonnais commanded the fleet that seized Madras; his subsequent quarrel with Dupleix over what to do with the city weakened French cohesion.
• C (Count de Lally) — 4 (Defeated at the Battle of Wandiwash, 1760): Lally arrived in 1758 with high hopes; his strategic errors — including recalling Bussy — culminated in decisive defeat at Wandiwash.
• D (Northern Circars) — 2 (Coastal Andhra territories that constituted France's principal territorial holding in India): Ceded to France through Bussy's influence over the Nizam; later transferred to the English EIC by the Nizam in 1765.

Value Addition:
• Lally was executed in France after his return — charged with betrayal; a reflection of how French civil-military coordination had broken down.
• Northern Circars passing to the English EIC in 1765 is contextually linked to the Diwani grant in Bengal — both consolidated English territorial power simultaneously.
• Bussy's recall to fight at Wandiwash is considered one of the most consequential strategic blunders of French India.

solution.concept_anchor: French institutional weakness vs EIC private structure
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a tempts students who know both facts are correct and assume institutional weakness automatically explains the recall without pausing to check whether R is the complete or exclusive causal explanation of A.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Dupleix was recalled by the French Compagnie in 1754 due to mounting costs of his territorial wars.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. The French Compagnie was state-controlled and financially dependent on the royal treasury, giving it far less financial autonomy than the privately-driven English EIC.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Partially but not completely. R describes a structural condition; the immediate cause of Dupleix's recall was also the Compagnie's deliberate preference for commerce over territorial ambition and the specific financial losses his campaigns generated. R is a contributing background factor, not the direct causal explanation of A. Both are correct, but R does not fully and directly explain A — option b.
Final check: Both A and R correct + R does NOT exclusively explain A → option b confirmed.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the 'Both correct but R doesn't explain A' option — the hardest assertion-reason outcome to select. Students who confirm both A and R are true instinctively choose option a. However, R describes a structural background condition (state vs private ownership) that predisposed the French Compagnie to financial caution, but the direct trigger for Dupleix's recall was the Compagnie's specific cost-benefit calculation about his campaigns — R is a background factor, not a direct causal explanation.
solution.final_explanation:
The recall of Dupleix in 1754 is one of the most analytically significant events of the Carnatic Wars, often examined through the institutional lens.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: The French Compagnie des Indes recalled Dupleix in 1754. The mounting financial losses from his territorial wars, combined with the Compagnie's preference for commerce over empire, made his continuation untenable.
• Reason (R) — Correct: The French Compagnie was indeed state-controlled and dependent on the royal treasury, giving it significantly less financial autonomy and risk appetite compared to the privately-owned, profit-driven English EIC.
• Causal relationship: R is true and contextually relevant but does not directly and exclusively explain A. R describes a structural predisposition; A was triggered by a specific cost-benefit decision about Dupleix's campaigns. The recall was caused by financial losses and institutional priorities — R is a background condition enabling that decision, not its direct cause.

Value Addition:
• Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) followed Dupleix's recall — both sides nominally agreed to non-interference in Indian politics, a provision neither fully honoured.
• No French successor to Dupleix matched his political vision — institutional weakness thus compounded personal replacement.
• English EIC's private ownership gave it the ability to reinvest profits rapidly and pursue aggressive strategies without waiting for metropolitan approval.

solution.concept_anchor: Second Carnatic War key events chronological sequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b tempts students who know Arcot came 'after' the Second Carnatic War began but misplace the death of Muzaffar Jung, placing it after Arcot when it actually preceded Clive's intervention.
elimination_logic: The Second Carnatic War began in 1749 with the opening of dual succession disputes — this anchors the start.
Muzaffar Jung was killed in 1751 while Bussy then secured French dominance in Hyderabad — this precedes the Arcot operation.
Clive's capture of Arcot occurred in September 1751 — after Muzaffar Jung's death earlier that year.

Chanda Sahib's capture and execution by Tanjore forces in 1752 came after Arcot's defence compelled him to redirect forces. Correct sequence: Outbreak of war (1749) → Death of Muzaffar Jung (1751) → Clive captures Arcot (September 1751) → Chanda Sahib executed (1752), pointing to option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap lies in Muzaffar Jung's death and Arcot both occurring in 1751 — students who know both events but not their sequence within that year will be tempted to reverse them. Option b exploits exactly this uncertainty. Additionally, placing Chanda Sahib's execution before Arcot (option a) is a classic reversal — Arcot's defence was precisely what unravelled Chanda Sahib's campaign.
solution.final_explanation:
The Second Carnatic War (1749–1754) featured a rapid sequence of interconnected events across two succession theatres — Carnatic and Hyderabad.

Correct sequence: 1 → 3 → 2 → 4
• Event 1 (Outbreak, 1749): The war began with French and English backing rival claimants — Chanda Sahib vs Anwaruddin/Muhammad Ali in Carnatic, Muzaffar Jung vs Nasir Jung in Hyderabad.
• Event 3 (Death of Muzaffar Jung, 1751): Muzaffar Jung was killed in an internal conflict; Bussy then secured French influence over his successor Salabat Jung, cementing French hold over Hyderabad.
• Event 2 (Arcot, September 1751): Clive's capture and defence of Arcot diverted Chanda Sahib's forces from Trichinopoly, turning the tide in the Carnatic theatre.
• Event 4 (Chanda Sahib executed, 1752): With his forces diverted and the English gaining momentum, Chanda Sahib was captured and executed by Tanjore forces — ending the French-backed Carnatic succession bid.

Value Addition:
• The year 1751 was the pivot of the Second Carnatic War — two major events (Muzaffar Jung's death and Arcot) both occurred within months of each other.
• Morari Rao's Marathas aided Clive during the Arcot defence, illustrating coalition-dependency.
• The Second Carnatic War ended with the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754), which proved unenforceable within two years.

solution.concept_anchor: Carnatic Wars as laboratory for British imperial methods
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d tempts students who associate 'British imperial expansion' exclusively with military conquest and overlook the proxy-war and alliance-manipulation dimensions that the Carnatic Wars specifically pioneered.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a European power backing a local claimant, providing military support in exchange for territorial concessions, then using the grateful ruler as a dependent ally — this is precisely the Carnatic Wars template.
Eliminate option a: Direct annexation is not described in the scenario; the European power works through a local ruler, not against him.
Eliminate option c: Doctrine of Lapse (attributable to Dalhousie, 1848 onwards) refers to annexing states of rulers who die without natural heirs — not applicable here.

Eliminate option d: Forward policy refers to expanding territorial boundaries to prevent rival powers from approaching — the scenario is about political manipulation through a claimant, not geographic buffer-seeking. Option b — the subsidiary alliance / proxy-support template from Carnatic Wars — correctly describes the scenario's logic.
solution.final_explanation:
The Carnatic Wars established a replicable template that the English EIC applied across India for the next century: identify a succession dispute, back one claimant with military support, defeat the rival, and extract territorial or financial concessions from the grateful winner — leaving him as a dependent ally.

The scenario describes exactly this mechanism. The European power does not conquer directly but operates through a pliant local ruler, gaining territory and influence without assuming full administrative responsibility.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Direct annexation removes the local ruler; the scenario explicitly retains the ruler as a dependent ally.
• Option (b): Correct. This is the proxy-support and subsidised alliance template pioneered during the Carnatic Wars — backing a claimant in exchange for concessions, then relying on his dependence. Later systematised as Subsidiary Alliance by Wellesley.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Doctrine of Lapse addresses inheritance failure, not contested succession with competing alive claimants.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Forward policy is a geographic-strategic concept about frontier expansion as a buffer against rival powers, not about manipulating succession disputes.

Value Addition:
• Muhammad Ali of Carnatic became exactly such a pliant English ally post-1752 — the template worked in practice.
• Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (1798) formalised this model: Indian rulers received British troops and surrendered foreign policy control.
• Marathas' failure to intervene decisively during Carnatic Wars allowed this template to become entrenched before they could counter it.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Paris 1763 French enclaves India
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Mahe) is deceptive because it is located on the Malabar (west) coast rather than the Coromandel (east) coast like most other French settlements, leading students to think geographic anomaly = odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify which settlements were returned to France as de-militarised trading posts under the Treaty of Paris (1763): Pondicherry, Karikal, Mahe, Chandernagore, and Yanam — five enclaves.
Pondicherry, Karikal, Mahe, Chandernagore are all among these five — each belongs to the list of French enclaves restored under Treaty of Paris.
Surat was never a French enclave — it was a major English and Mughal trading port; the French had no significant territorial holding there.
Surat does not belong to the same category as the others, confirming option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the geographic confusion between Mahe (west coast, Malabar) and the east-coast French settlements. Students may incorrectly flag Mahe as the odd one out because it is geographically distinct from Pondicherry and Karikal. In reality, Mahe is firmly among the five French enclaves restored under the Treaty of Paris (1763). Surat, though a famous trading port, was never a French territorial holding — making it the true outlier.
solution.final_explanation:
The Treaty of Paris (1763) restored five French settlements in India — but with a critical restriction: they could not be fortified or used for stationing troops, reducing them to purely commercial enclaves.

• Option (a) — Pondicherry: Belongs. The headquarters of French India and their most important settlement, restored under the Treaty of Paris.
• Option (b) — Mahe: Belongs. Located on the Malabar coast (west), Mahe was one of the five French enclaves restored. Its west-coast location makes it geographically distinct but not categorically different.
• Option (c) — Surat: Does NOT belong. Surat was a major English and Mughal/Maratha commercial port. The French had no significant territorial holding at Surat; it was never part of the French enclave network.
• Option (d) — Chandernagore: Belongs. Located in Bengal, Chandernagore was the French settlement in eastern India, also restored under the Treaty of Paris.

Value Addition:
• The five French enclaves under Treaty of Paris: Pondicherry, Karikal, Mahe, Chandernagore, Yanam.
• These enclaves remained French territories until 1954, when they merged with independent India.
• The de-militarisation condition was the key restriction — France kept the name but lost the power.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Paris 1763 vs Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle 1748 contrast

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) restored the status quo ante in India, returning Madras to England in exchange for Louisbourg in Canada, leaving the fundamental balance of power between the English and French in India unchanged.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle restored the pre-war territorial positions and was a status quo settlement — it did not permanently alter the balance; both sides resumed rivalry almost immediately in the Second Carnatic War.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Paris (1763) expelled France completely from India, terminating all French territorial presence on the subcontinent.
statement_analysis.reason: France was NOT expelled entirely; it retained five enclaves (Pondicherry, Karikal, Mahe, Chandernagore, Yanam) — but they were de-militarised, meaning France could not fortify them or station troops, reducing them to commercial-only posts.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a ('Both correct') tempts students who know the Treaty of Paris fundamentally weakened France and loosely recall 'France lost India' without remembering the de-militarisation nuance that preserved five enclaves.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) was indeed a status quo treaty — Madras for Louisbourg, no permanent territorial change. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Treaty of Paris did NOT expel France completely — five enclaves were retained, albeit de-militarised. 'Terminated all French territorial presence' is factually wrong. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains the classic scope-extension trap: 'expelled France completely' overstates what the Treaty of Paris actually did. France retained five de-militarised enclaves. Students who have absorbed the general conclusion that 'France lost India after 1763' may not recall the precise condition — retention without military capacity. This distinction is a high-frequency UPSC discrimination point.
solution.final_explanation:
The two treaties bookending the Carnatic Wars represent starkly different outcomes for the Anglo-French rivalry.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) was a status quo ante restoration. Madras was exchanged for Louisbourg in Canada with no lasting change in the Indian balance — both sides resumed competition in the Second Carnatic War almost immediately.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Treaty of Paris (1763) did not expel France from India. It restored Pondicherry, Karikal, Mahe, Chandernagore, and Yanam to French possession — but imposed the critical condition that none could be fortified or used for troop deployment. France retained a nominal territorial presence but lost all political-military relevance.

Value Addition:
• The de-militarisation condition in the Treaty of Paris is the single most important distinction between 'expelled' and 'neutralised' — France was neutralised, not expelled.
• French enclaves remained under French sovereignty until 1954, eventually merging with independent India.
• The contrast between 1748 (status quo) and 1763 (permanent alteration) is a favourite UPSC analytical pairing.

solution.concept_anchor: Clive EIC career trajectory Carnatic to Bengal
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c ('military officer') is deceptive because students associate Clive entirely with military exploits and may not know his original civilian designation within the EIC hierarchy.
elimination_logic: Identify Clive's original role: he joined the EIC not as a soldier but in an administrative-commercial capacity — as a 'writer' (clerk).
Eliminate 'military officer' (c): his initial appointment was civilian; the military role came later.
Eliminate 'surgeon' (d) and 'factor' (a): these are plausible EIC designations but historically incorrect for Clive's entry-level position.
Clive joined as a 'writer' — the lowest rung of EIC civilian service — before transitioning to military command. Option b is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the instinctive association of Clive with military identity. Students who know Clive primarily as a general assume he began as a military officer. In fact, he was initially employed as a 'writer' — the EIC's term for a junior clerk — and transitioned to military duties during the First Carnatic War when the company needed men to fight.
solution.final_explanation:
Robert Clive's trajectory is one of the most remarkable transformations in Indian colonial history — from junior administrative employee to the architect of British power in India.

• Option (a) — factor: Incorrect. A 'factor' was a senior merchant or trading agent in the EIC hierarchy — Clive's entry position was below this rank.
• Option (b) — writer: Correct. 'Writer' was the lowest civilian grade in the EIC service — essentially a junior clerk. Clive joined in this capacity and transitioned to military duties during the First Carnatic War when the company urgently needed personnel.
• Option (c) — military officer: Incorrect. Though Clive became famous as a commander, his original appointment was civilian. Assuming a military entry reflects familiarity with his later career but not his starting point.
• Option (d) — surgeon: Incorrect. Surgeons were specialist employees in the EIC's medical establishment — a separate career track entirely.

Value Addition:
• The EIC civilian hierarchy: Writer → Factor → Senior Merchant — Clive began at the very bottom.
• Clive's military breakthrough came at the Siege of Arcot (1751), followed by Plassey (1757) — his Bengal operation that founded British territorial empire.
• Clive served two separate tenures as Governor of Bengal (1757–60 and 1765–67).

solution.concept_anchor: Naval engagements Anglo-French rivalry commanders
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because Eyre Coote and Wandiwash is a well-known pair, but the question asks about naval engagements — Wandiwash was a land battle, making this pairing categorically wrong for the naval dimension.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option c: Wandiwash (1760) was a land battle between Coote and Lally — it is not a naval engagement.
Eliminate option d: Cuddalore (1758) was a French naval engagement but it was commanded by Comte d'Aché, not Bussy — Bussy was a land commander stationed in Hyderabad.
Eliminate option b: La Bourdonnais captured Madras (1746) — this is correct. But the option pairs him with 'Battle of Cuddalore' when he was associated with the capture of Madras, not Cuddalore.
Confirm option a: La Bourdonnais commanding the French naval force that captured Madras in 1746 is historically accurate — this is the correctly matched naval pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option c exploits the fact that Eyre Coote and Wandiwash is a famous pair — but Wandiwash was a land battle, not a naval engagement. The question specifically asks about naval engagement pairs. Students who identify the famous pair without reading 'naval engagement' will be caught by this domain-specificity trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The naval dimension of the Carnatic Wars is frequently underemphasised but critical to understanding why French land victories could not be consolidated.

• Option (a): Correctly matched. La Bourdonnais commanded the French fleet that captured Madras from the English in 1746 — the opening naval success of the First Carnatic War. His subsequent quarrel with Dupleix over ransoming Madras weakened French strategic cohesion.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. La Bourdonnais is paired with the Battle of Cuddalore — but Cuddalore (1758) was a different naval engagement; La Bourdonnais's famous operation was the capture of Madras (1746).
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched. Eyre Coote and Wandiwash (1760) is a famous pairing — but Wandiwash was a land battle, not a naval engagement.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. Bussy was France's most effective land commander in Hyderabad; he had no significant naval command role at Cuddalore.

Value Addition:
• English naval superiority in the Indian Ocean meant French land victories (like Cuddalore 1758) were strategically sterile — no reinforcements could consolidate them.
• The internal dispute between La Bourdonnais and Dupleix over Madras's fate (ransom vs retention) is a telling example of French command fragmentation.
• English sea control after 1757 globally (Seven Years' War) made the French position in India structurally unviable.

solution.concept_anchor: Carnatic region political structure power vacuum causes

statement_analysis.statement: The Carnatic region was nominally under Mughal suzerainty exercised through the Hyderabad Nizam but had become practically autonomous by the early eighteenth century.
statement_analysis.reason: After Aurangzeb's death, the Mughal grip over the Deccan and Carnatic weakened rapidly; the Carnatic Nawab operated with near-total independence even as he retained nominal subordination to the Nizam who in turn owed nominal allegiance to the Mughal emperor.

statement_analysis.statement: The proximity of Madras and Pondicherry — both located on the Coromandel Coast and approximately 160 km apart — made direct Anglo-French competition in the Carnatic region structurally inevitable.
statement_analysis.reason: With both European bases on the same coastal strip, separated by roughly 160 km, each power's expansion directly threatened the other's commercial and political interests, making sustained rivalry almost unavoidable.

statement_analysis.statement: The three-way power structure of the Carnatic Nawab, the Hyderabad Nizam, and the Maratha Confederacy provided Europeans with only a single point of intervention, making their political strategy straightforward.
statement_analysis.reason: The three-way structure actually provided Europeans with multiple intervention points — any two of the three regional powers could be courted against the third, making European political manipulation more complex and rewarding, not simpler.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d ('1, 2 and 3') tempts students who know the three-way structure is important and assume any true-sounding statement about it must be correct, without catching the reversal in Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Carnatic as practically autonomous under nominal Mughal-Nizam suzerainty is well-established for the early 18th century — correct.
Confirm Statement 2: Madras (English) and Pondicherry (French) approximately 160 km apart on the same coast — structural inevitability of rivalry — correct.
Reject Statement 3: The three-way structure provided multiple intervention points, not a single one — the word 'only a single point' makes this factually inverted. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, 3 incorrect → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses 'only a single point of intervention' — a scope-reduction inversion of the actual historical reality. The three-way power structure (Carnatic Nawab + Nizam + Marathas) was precisely what made European manipulation so effective: multiple alliance options, multiple succession disputes to exploit. Students who read quickly may not catch this inversion.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the structural conditions of the Carnatic region explains why it became the primary arena for Anglo-French conflict rather than Bengal or the Malabar coast.

• Statement 1 — Correct: By the early 18th century, Mughal authority in the south had collapsed. The Carnatic Nawab's practical autonomy — despite nominal Mughal-via-Nizam suzerainty — created exactly the kind of power vacuum that competing European powers could exploit.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The ~160 km distance between Madras and Pondicherry on the same Coromandel coastal strip made the two powers immediate neighbours. Each company's commercial expansion necessarily encroached on the other's sphere — geographic proximity was itself a cause of rivalry.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The three-way regional structure (Carnatic Nawab, Hyderabad Nizam, Maratha Confederacy) offered Europeans multiple, not one, intervention points. Any regional actor could be courted against another — this multiplicity was a structural advantage for manipulation, not a limitation.

Value Addition:
• Arcot's importance as the Carnatic Nawab's capital meant control of Arcot conferred political legitimacy across the entire region.
• Hyderabad's Nizam was a separate and often decisive actor — Bussy's influence there gave France a Deccan foothold independent of the Carnatic theatre.
• Maratha neutrality or selective alignment during the Carnatic Wars was a key variable both sides tried to influence.

solution.concept_anchor: Lally strategic errors French failure Third Carnatic War

statement_analysis.statement: Count de Lally's recall of Marquis de Bussy from Hyderabad to reinforce the Wandiwash campaign is considered a strategic blunder because it simultaneously weakened French political influence in the Deccan and deprived the battlefield of France's most experienced Indian-theatre commander.
statement_analysis.reason: This dual damage — loss of political influence in Hyderabad and removal of Bussy from his most effective theatre — is the standard historical assessment of Lally's strategic error.

statement_analysis.statement: Lally's failure at the siege of Madras (1758–59) was primarily due to a shortage of artillery rather than any deficiency in infantry strength or supply lines.
statement_analysis.reason: Lally's failure at Madras resulted from a combination of factors including inadequate naval support (English sea control disrupted supply), internal conflicts with French councillors at Pondicherry, and supply chain problems — attributing it 'primarily' to artillery shortage is an oversimplification that ignores the dominant structural causes.

statement_analysis.statement: After his return to France, Lally was executed on charges of betrayal — a judgment widely regarded as politically motivated and controversial rather than a fair reflection of his military conduct in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Lally was indeed executed in France; historians and contemporaries noted that his execution reflected political blame-shifting rather than a fair assessment of his actual conduct, which was hampered by institutional and supply failures beyond his sole control.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b ('1 only') misleads students who know Statement 1 is definitely correct and assume Statement 3 — Lally's controversial execution — is also correct, leaving them uncertain whether Statement 2's artillery claim might also be true.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Recalling Bussy as a dual strategic error (Deccan + battlefield) is standard historical consensus — Statement 1 is correct.

Scrutinise Statement 2: 'Primarily due to artillery shortage' is an unsupported oversimplification; the failure at Madras involved naval supply disruption, internal administrative conflict, and logistical collapse — Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Confirm Statement 3: Lally's execution in France as a controversial politically motivated judgment is historically documented — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct → option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's trap is the use of 'primarily' — a scope word that converts a partial truth into a false statement. Artillery was one element of Lally's difficulties, but the dominant factors were English naval superiority disrupting supply, internal civil-military conflict with French councillors, and logistical failures. Students who vaguely remember 'Lally had supply problems' may not isolate artillery as an over-specific and incorrect attribution.
solution.final_explanation:
Count de Lally's campaign (1758–1761) is a case study in how institutional dysfunction amplifies battlefield misfortune.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Recalling Bussy from Hyderabad was Lally's most consequential error. It simultaneously ended seven years of French political dominance in the Deccan (through the Nizam's court) and removed France's most capable Indian-theatre field commander for a battle — Wandiwash — that Lally then lost.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The failure at Madras (1758–59) cannot be attributed 'primarily' to an artillery shortage. The dominant causes were English naval control disrupting French supply lines, Lally's toxic relationship with French civilian councillors at Pondicherry who withheld resources, and overall logistical breakdown. 'Artillery shortage' as the primary cause is historically unsupported.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Lally was executed in France after his return — charged with betrayal. Even contemporaries found the verdict unjust, recognising that he had operated under severe institutional constraints that no individual commander could fully overcome.

Value Addition:
• Lally's execution was later overturned posthumously — Voltaire campaigned for his rehabilitation.
• The conflict between Lally and the Pondicherry Council reflects the broader dysfunction of French civil-military coordination in India.
• English success in the Third Carnatic War owed as much to French self-sabotage as to English military prowess.

solution.concept_anchor: Chanda Sahib fate capture execution 1752
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (executed by Hyderabad forces) tempts students who know 'Chanda Sahib was killed by Indian forces' but are imprecise about which Indian power was responsible — Hyderabad was France's ally, making it a particularly devious swap.
elimination_logic: Chanda Sahib was the French-backed claimant to the Carnatic Nawabship; his campaign unravelled after Clive's Arcot operation.
Eliminate option a: Hyderabad under Muzaffar Jung was France's ally — it would not have executed Chanda Sahib.
Eliminate option c: Chanda Sahib was not executed on Dupleix's orders — this is fabricated.

Eliminate option d: Maratha forces under Morari Rao aided the English but the execution was carried out by Tanjore, not the broader Maratha Confederacy leadership. Tanjore forces captured and executed Chanda Sahib in 1752 — option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces 'Tanjore forces' with 'Hyderabad forces' in option a. This is particularly vicious because students know Hyderabad was France's ally — so they might dismiss a too-obvious 'enemy executed him' answer and search for a more complex explanation, landing on option a as a 'sophisticated' wrong choice. Tanjore, not Hyderabad, was the power that held and executed Chanda Sahib.
solution.final_explanation:
Chanda Sahib's fate illustrates how completely the French-backed strategy in the Carnatic collapsed after Clive's Arcot intervention.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Hyderabad — under French ally Muzaffar Jung and later Salabat Jung under Bussy's influence — was firmly in the French camp. It had no motive to execute Chanda Sahib.
• Option (b): Correct. After his campaign collapsed in 1752, Chanda Sahib was captured and executed by the forces of the Raja of Tanjore — a regional power that had remained outside the main Franco-British contest and chose to eliminate a destabilising claimant.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Dupleix did not order Chanda Sahib's execution — this claim has no historical basis.
• Option (d): Incorrect. While Maratha forces (Morari Rao) had cooperated with the English against Chanda Sahib, it was specifically Tanjore forces — not the broader Maratha Confederacy — that executed him.

Value Addition:
• Chanda Sahib's execution in 1752 effectively ended the Second Carnatic War's first phase — Muhammad Ali, the English-backed claimant, was now undisputed Nawab of Carnatic.
• Tanjore (Thanjavur) was a semi-independent Maratha principality in the far south — distinct from the main Peshwa-led Confederacy.
• Chanda Sahib had been a prisoner of the Marathas earlier (before the Second Carnatic War) — making his life a series of captivities.

solution.concept_anchor: Bussy Hyderabad Northern Circars French territorial legacy

statement_analysis.statement: Marquis de Bussy's influence in Hyderabad between 1751 and 1758 was so pervasive that he effectively controlled Deccan politics through the Nizam Salabat Jung, making this the high point of French political power in peninsular India.
statement_analysis.reason: Bussy's seven years in Hyderabad — securing the Northern Circars, managing court politics, and directing military deployments — represented France's greatest territorial and political achievement in India.

statement_analysis.statement: The Northern Circars, ceded to France as a result of Bussy's influence over the Nizam, were subsequently transferred to the English East India Company by the Nizam in 1765, making them part of the early territorial foundations of British power in coastal Andhra.
statement_analysis.reason: After French power collapsed, the Nizam ceded the Northern Circars to the English EIC in 1765 — the same year as the Diwani grant in Bengal — extending British coastal control southward.

statement_analysis.statement: Bussy's recall to fight at Wandiwash in 1760 was strategically sound because Hyderabad's political situation had already stabilised sufficiently to allow French forces to be redeployed.
statement_analysis.reason: Historians uniformly regard Bussy's recall as a strategic blunder — Hyderabad had not stabilised; without French military presence, the Nizam rapidly moved toward the English. The recall weakened both fronts simultaneously.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d ('1, 2 and 3') tempts students who accept that Bussy's recall 'must have been justified' given Lally's overall command, and don't scrutinise Statement 3's characterisation of the recall as 'strategically sound.'
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Bussy's 1751–1758 period in Hyderabad as France's political apex in the Deccan is textbook — correct.
Confirm Statement 2: Northern Circars transferred to English EIC in 1765 by the Nizam — correct and important for understanding British coastal consolidation.
Reject Statement 3: Bussy's recall is universally assessed as a strategic blunder, not a sound decision — Hyderabad was not stabilised and the recall weakened both fronts. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, 3 incorrect → option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3's trap is the deliberate inversion of historical consensus — framing a notorious strategic blunder as 'strategically sound.' Students who know Bussy was recalled but do not have precise knowledge of why historians consider it disastrous may find the 'stabilised sufficiently' qualifier plausible and accept Statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Bussy's period in Hyderabad represents both the apex of French influence in India and, through his mishandled recall, the beginning of its collapse.

• Statement 1 — Correct: From 1751 to 1758, Bussy's manipulation of Nizam Salabat Jung's court gave France unparalleled political leverage in the Deccan — access to revenue, military support, and the Northern Circars as territorial compensation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Northern Circars (coastal Andhra — roughly modern Visakhapatnam, Rajahmundry, and Eluru districts) passed to the English EIC through a Nizam's grant in 1765. This chronologically coincides with the Diwani grant in Bengal, marking a simultaneous consolidation of British power on two fronts.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Bussy's recall to fight at Wandiwash was not strategically sound. Hyderabad had not stabilised — removing French troops created an immediate political vacuum that the English exploited to pull the Nizam into their orbit. The recall damaged both the Deccan front and the Wandiwash battle, which was still lost.

Value Addition:
• The Northern Circars' transfer (1765) is an early example of British coastal strategy — connecting Bengal-based power with south Indian presence.
• Bussy is often called France's most effective operator in India — his removal is cited as the decisive turning point of the Third Carnatic War.
• Salabat Jung (Nizam) ruled with French backing; after Bussy left, he was increasingly marginalised within his own court.

solution.concept_anchor: EIC private ownership financial autonomy vs French state company
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a tempts students who correctly identify both A and R as true and instinctively link institutional structure to commercial outcomes without pausing to verify whether R specifically explains A or only provides related background.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. The English EIC was a jointly-owned private company; profits were reinvested by shareholders and the company operated with substantial commercial autonomy.

Step 2: Is R correct? — No. Claiming the French Compagnie was 'never profitable at any point in its history' is an overstatement; the Compagnie did generate profits in earlier phases, particularly in the late 17th century. The accurate claim is that it was financially constrained and dependent on the royal treasury during the critical Carnatic Wars period, not that it was perpetually unprofitable.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer is c (A correct, R incorrect).
Final check: A correct + R incorrect → option c confirmed.
solution.final_explanation:
The institutional contrast between the two East India companies is one of the most important analytical explanations for why England, not France, won the Carnatic Wars.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: The English EIC was a privately held joint-stock company. Shareholders had strong incentives to maximise profit, and the company could make rapid commercial and strategic decisions without waiting for government approval. Profits were reinvested, enabling continuous expansion.
• Reason (R) — Incorrect: While the French Compagnie was indeed state-controlled and financially weaker than the English EIC during the Carnatic Wars, the claim that it was 'never profitable at any point in its history' is factually wrong. The Compagnie had profitable phases, particularly in earlier decades. The accurate characterisation is that it was financially constrained and treasury-dependent during the critical mid-18th century period — not perpetually unprofitable throughout its existence.

Value Addition:
• The English EIC's private ownership also meant it could raise credit in London's capital markets more easily than the French Compagnie could access the French royal treasury.
• Lord Wellesley's aggressive expansion (1798–1805) was itself partly financed by EIC commercial revenues — demonstrating how private profit-orientation enabled imperial expansion.
• State ownership of the French Compagnie meant commercial policy was subject to political priorities — trade vs. empire tensions were resolved in favour of trade, costing France the subcontinent.

solution.concept_anchor: Third Carnatic War key events correct sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c tempts students who know Wandiwash preceded the fall of Pondicherry but misplace the capture of Fort St. David — assuming it happened after Lally's arrival but before Wandiwash, without knowing the gap between these events.
elimination_logic: The Seven Years' War began in 1756 — this opens the Third Carnatic War's global context.
Count de Lally arrived in India in 1758 and promptly captured Fort St. David — his early success.
Battle of Wandiwash was fought on January 22, 1760 — the decisive English victory.

Fall of Pondicherry occurred in 1761 after the French could no longer resupply it. Correct order: Seven Years' War outbreak (1756) → Lally captures Fort St. David (1758) → Battle of Wandiwash (1760) → Fall of Pondicherry (1761) → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the 1758 placement of Fort St. David's capture. Students who know Lally arrived in 1758 and Wandiwash was in 1760 may correctly sequence those two, but confuse whether Fort St. David came before or after Wandiwash. The answer is before — it was Lally's early success in 1758, not a post-Wandiwash event.
solution.final_explanation:
The Third Carnatic War (1756–1763) unfolded over nearly a decade across two continents, with the Indian theatre playing out in a clear sequence.

Correct sequence: 1 → 3 → 4 → 2
• Event 1 (Seven Years' War, 1756): The global conflict between Britain and France began, automatically extending the truce between their Indian companies and reopening hostilities in the Carnatic.
• Event 3 (Lally captures Fort St. David, 1758): Lally arrived with fresh troops and initial momentum — capturing Fort St. David (near Cuddalore) was his opening success before the campaign turned against France.
• Event 4 (Battle of Wandiwash, January 22, 1760): Sir Eyre Coote's decisive victory destroyed French offensive capacity; Bussy was captured and Lally's army broken.
• Event 2 (Fall of Pondicherry, 1761): Stripped of the ability to receive naval reinforcements and having lost at Wandiwash, Pondicherry fell and was subsequently razed by the English.

Value Addition:
• Fort St. David (near Cuddalore) was an English fortification — its capture by Lally in 1758 was a significant early French success that misled observers about French chances.
• Pondicherry's razing in 1761 was a deliberate English act to prevent its future use as a military base — it was later rebuilt and returned under the Treaty of Paris (1763).
• The Seven Years' War (1756–63) is called the 'first world war' by some historians — fought across Europe, Americas, Africa, India, and the Philippines simultaneously.

solution.concept_anchor: Wellesley formalises subsidiary alliance Dupleix as originator
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Dupleix as originator and formaliser) is deceptive because students who know 'Dupleix started the subsidiary alliance idea' may not distinguish between conceptual origin and formal systematisation, and select b as the comprehensive answer.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a formal, institutionalised system applied systematically to multiple rulers with standardised terms — this signals 'formalisation', not informal ad hoc application.
Eliminate option a: The scenario explicitly states the system was 'standardised' and 'formally applied' — this goes beyond Dupleix's informal Carnatic Wars practices.
Eliminate option b: While Dupleix originated the concept informally, formal systematisation is attributed to Wellesley — option b conflates origin with formalisation.
Eliminate option c: The scenario involves maintaining a local ruler as a dependent ally — this is not the Doctrine of Lapse, which addresses heirless successions.
Option d correctly identifies Wellesley as the formaliser while acknowledging Dupleix as conceptual originator — the historically accurate analytical answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Dupleix for Wellesley as the 'formaliser.' Students who know Dupleix 'originated' the concept may select option b without registering that the scenario describes a standardised, institutionalised system — which points to Wellesley's formal Subsidiary Alliance, not Dupleix's ad hoc Carnatic interventions.
solution.final_explanation:
The Subsidiary Alliance system is one of the most consequential instruments of British imperial expansion, and its intellectual lineage connects the Carnatic Wars to Wellesley's formidable imperial project.

The scenario describes a formalised, standardised system: a European power provides troops to an Indian ruler, who cedes territory/revenue and surrenders foreign policy control, becoming a guaranteed-but-dependent sovereign. This is the Subsidiary Alliance in its mature form.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Dupleix's practices in the Carnatic Wars were informal and context-specific — not a standardised system applied consistently across multiple rulers.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Dupleix did originate the conceptual template, but he did not formally systematise it — the 'formal' element in the scenario points to Wellesley.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie, 1848+) addresses heirless successions — irrelevant to the scenario's competition between alive claimants.
• Option (d): Correct. The Subsidiary Alliance was formally systematised by Lord Wellesley from 1798, with standardised terms applied to Hyderabad (1798), Mysore (1799), and the Marathas (1802). Its conceptual ancestry traces to Dupleix's Carnatic practices — making option d the complete, analytically accurate answer.

Value Addition:
• Under Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance, Indian rulers paid for British troops stationed in their territories — the cost burden itself weakened their finances over time.
• Hyderabad was the first to sign (1798) — the same Nizam's court where Bussy had built French influence four decades earlier.
• The Carnatic Wars are thus directly connected to Wellesley's imperial project through this institutional lineage.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
An eighteenth-century European power operating in India developed a formal system under which it provided military contingents to Indian rulers facing internal or external threats. In exchange, the Indian ruler ceded revenue from specific territories to fund the troops and agreed not to conduct independent foreign policy or enter alliances with other powers. The European power guaranteed the ruler's security and sovereignty against other threats. This system was standardised and formally applied to multiple Indian rulers, transforming them into dependent allies.

Which of the following most accurately identifies the origin and formalisation of the system described in the scenario?

(a) The system was originated and fully formalised by Dupleix during the Carnatic Wars (1746–1754) as a deliberate instrument of French imperial expansion
(b) The system was originated by Dupleix during the Carnatic Wars and further developed by him into a standardised framework before his recall in 1754
(c) The system corresponds to the Doctrine of Lapse and was formalised by Lord Dalhousie in the mid-nineteenth century
(d) The system's conceptual template was first practised informally by Dupleix during the Carnatic Wars but was formally systematised as the Subsidiary Alliance by Lord Wellesley from 1798 onwards

solution.concept_anchor: Battle of St Thome First Carnatic War European military superiority

statement_analysis.statement: The Battle of St. Thome (1746) demonstrated that a smaller European-trained force could defeat a substantially larger Indian army, undermining the assumption that numerical superiority alone determined military outcomes in India.
statement_analysis.reason: French forces under Paradis defeated Nawab Anwaruddin's far larger army at St. Thome — this engagement is historically cited as the earliest clear demonstration of European tactical superiority over Indian forces in the Carnatic.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Carnatic War (1746–1748) was triggered by the outbreak of the Seven Years' War in Europe, which automatically extended hostilities between England and France to their Indian trading settlements.
statement_analysis.reason: The First Carnatic War was triggered by the War of Austrian Succession (1740–1748), not the Seven Years' War (1756–1763) — the Seven Years' War was the backdrop of the Third Carnatic War.

statement_analysis.statement: French commander Peyton was defeated by the French fleet before Madras fell, allowing Dupleix to proceed with the capture of the city.
statement_analysis.reason: Peyton was the English naval commander — he chose to withdraw rather than engage the French fleet (under La Bourdonnais), effectively abandoning Madras. He was not 'defeated' in battle but retreated, allowing the French to proceed unchallenged.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Carnatic War ended with both sides restoring their pre-war territorial positions, leaving the fundamental balance of European power in India unchanged.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) was a status quo restoration — Madras returned to England in exchange for Louisbourg, with no permanent shift in the Indian balance. Both sides resumed competition almost immediately.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c ('Only three') traps students who confidently accept Statement 1 and 4 as correct, then accept either Statement 2 or 3 as a 'third correct' by confusing Seven Years' War with War of Austrian Succession, or by misremembering Peyton as 'defeated in battle.'
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: St. Thome (1746) as proof of European tactical superiority — correct.
Reject Statement 2: First Carnatic War was triggered by War of Austrian Succession, not Seven Years' War — incorrect.
Reject Statement 3: Peyton retreated/withdrew; he was not defeated in open battle — the word 'defeated' mischaracterises his action — incorrect.
Confirm Statement 4: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) as a status quo restoration — correct. Only Statements 1 and 4 correct → Only two → option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses a temporal-swap — substituting the Seven Years' War (Third Carnatic War trigger) for the War of Austrian Succession (First Carnatic War trigger). This is one of the most tested confusions in the Carnatic Wars topic. Statement 3's trap is subtler — Peyton did exist and did fail to defend Madras, but he withdrew rather than being defeated in engagement. 'Defeated' makes Statement 3 a partial-truth distortion.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Carnatic War is foundational to understanding the Carnatic Wars but contains several precision traps.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Battle of St. Thome (1746) showed a smaller French force under Paradis routing Nawab Anwaruddin's larger army — the first major demonstration of European tactical advantage in southern India.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The First Carnatic War's European trigger was the War of Austrian Succession (1740–48). The Seven Years' War (1756–63) triggered the Third Carnatic War — a classic temporal-swap error.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Peyton was the English naval commander who chose to withdraw from Madras rather than risk battle against La Bourdonnais's fleet. Describing this as being 'defeated' overstates the engagement — there was no decisive naval battle; Peyton retreated, abandoning Madras.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) restored pre-war positions on both sides — Madras exchanged for Louisbourg — leaving the Indian balance of power structurally unchanged and setting the stage for renewed competition.

Value Addition:
• War of Austrian Succession → First Carnatic War; Seven Years' War → Third Carnatic War — a pairing worth memorising precisely.
• Battle of St. Thome (1746) is sometimes called the 'first battle to demonstrate European military superiority in the Carnatic.'
• Nawab Anwaruddin, defeated at St. Thome, was killed later (1749) at Ambur — another event in the Second Carnatic War succession dispute.

solution.concept_anchor: Maratha role Carnatic Wars coalition dependency Europeans

statement_analysis.statement: During the Carnatic Wars, both the English and French sought Maratha support, and Morari Rao's Maratha contingent ultimately aligned with the English and provided crucial assistance during the defence of Arcot.
statement_analysis.reason: Both European powers courted Maratha alliances; Morari Rao sided with the English and did provide support during Arcot's defence — this is historically documented.

statement_analysis.statement: The Maratha Confederacy's decisive military intervention during the Carnatic Wars prevented either European power from establishing dominance in southern India, preserving a balance of power until the late eighteenth century.
statement_analysis.reason: The Marathas did not intervene decisively or systematically to prevent European dominance; their engagement was tactical and opportunistic. English dominance was established by 1763 — the Marathas' failure to mount a concerted counter was itself a strategic failure that allowed singular European dominance to emerge.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a ('Both correct') tempts students who know Maratha involvement was real and significant, and assume that 'significant involvement' = 'decisive prevention of dominance' — conflating tactical participation with strategic impact.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Morari Rao's alignment with English during Arcot is documented — Statement 1 is correct.

Scrutinise Statement 2: 'Decisive military intervention... prevented either power from establishing dominance' — this overstates Maratha impact; English dominance was clearly established by 1763 without Maratha prevention. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses scope-extension — inflating tactical Maratha participation into a 'decisive intervention that prevented dominance.' Students who know Marathas were involved and important may not pause to test whether 'prevented dominance' is accurate. Given that English dominance was firmly established by 1763, Statement 2's claim is demonstrably false as a historical outcome.
solution.final_explanation:
Maratha involvement in the Carnatic Wars is a nuanced topic — present but not decisive in determining the final outcome.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Both European powers actively courted Maratha support, recognising that Maratha military power could tip the balance in the Carnatic. Morari Rao's contingent aligned with the English and aided Clive during the defence of Arcot — a genuine, documented contribution.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Marathas never mounted a systematic, decisive intervention designed to prevent either European power from dominating southern India. Their participation was tactical, opportunistic, and episodic. By 1763, English dominance over the Carnatic was uncontested — a clear refutation of Statement 2's claim that Maratha intervention 'preserved a balance of power.'

Value Addition:
• The Marathas' strategic failure during the Carnatic Wars — not exploiting the opportunity to prevent singular European dominance — is a recurring UPSC analytical theme.
• After the Carnatic Wars, the Marathas themselves became the primary target of English expansion through the three Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1782, 1803–1805, 1817–1818).
• Morari Rao is one of the few named Indian commanders on the English side during the Carnatic Wars — worth remembering for precision questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Pondicherry 1754 non-interference agreement
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c ('Treaty of Paris') is deceptive because it is the most famous treaty associated with French India, and students may assume it is the treaty that followed Dupleix's recall — when in fact that treaty was the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754), with the Treaty of Paris coming nine years later.
elimination_logic: Dupleix was recalled in 1754 — the treaty that followed his recall and attempted to codify non-interference was signed the same year.
Eliminate Treaty of Paris (c): that is the 1763 settlement ending the Third Carnatic War — nine years after Dupleix's recall.
Eliminate Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (b): that ended the First Carnatic War in 1748 — not related to Dupleix's recall.
Eliminate Convention of Masulipatnam (d): this is a plausible-sounding but fabricated treaty name for this context. The correct answer is Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) — option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap substitutes Treaty of Paris (1763) for Treaty of Pondicherry (1754). The Treaty of Paris is the most prominent treaty students associate with French India, making it the instinctive but wrong choice when any 'French-English treaty in India' question appears. The Treaty of Pondicherry was the immediate post-Dupleix settlement — far less famous, far more frequently confused.
solution.final_explanation:
The aftermath of Dupleix's recall was formalised through a specific treaty that students frequently overlook in favour of the more prominent Treaty of Paris.

• Option (a) — Treaty of Pondicherry (1754): Correct. Following Dupleix's recall, both sides signed the Treaty of Pondicherry, which nominally committed them to non-interference in Indian political affairs. In practice, it was almost immediately violated as both sides continued to support their respective allies.
• Option (b) — Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle: Incorrect. This 1748 treaty ended the First Carnatic War and the War of Austrian Succession in Europe — it pre-dates Dupleix's recall by six years.
• Option (c) — Treaty of Paris: Incorrect. The Treaty of Paris (1763) ended the Third Carnatic War and the Seven Years' War globally — nine years after Dupleix's recall.
• Option (d) — Convention of Masulipatnam: Incorrect. No such treaty formalised the post-Dupleix settlement.

Value Addition:
• The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) is notable precisely because it was unenforceable — the Third Carnatic War broke out just two years later in 1756.
• Pondicherry served as the capital of French India — having a treaty named after it while being the French headquarters adds to student confusion.
• Dupleix's successor as French Governor in India, Godeheu, negotiated the Treaty of Pondicherry — he lacked Dupleix's vision and accepted unfavourable terms.

solution.concept_anchor: Second Carnatic War succession claimants European backing
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Muzaffar Jung backed by English) is deceptive because students who remember Muzaffar Jung and Hyderabad as key figures may confuse which European power backed him — it was France, not England.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Muzaffar Jung was backed by France (with Dupleix's support), not England — this is an entity-swap.
Eliminate option b: Nasir Jung was supported by England — pairing him with French backing is a direct reversal.
Confirm option c: Muhammad Ali was the English-backed claimant to the Carnatic Nawabship — he is the correct English-supported figure in the Carnatic succession dispute.

Eliminate option d: Anwaruddin was the incumbent Carnatic Nawab who was killed at Ambur (1749) by Chanda Sahib's forces; he was supported by English earlier but was not a 'claimant' — his son Muhammad Ali became the English-backed claimant after his death. Option c is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap operates by mixing up the Carnatic and Hyderabad succession claimants and their European backers. Students who remember names like Muzaffar Jung, Nasir Jung, Chanda Sahib, and Muhammad Ali but are imprecise about which power backed which claimant will be vulnerable to options a and b. The key pairs to remember: French backed Chanda Sahib (Carnatic) + Muzaffar Jung (Hyderabad); English backed Muhammad Ali (Carnatic) + Nasir Jung (Hyderabad).
solution.final_explanation:
The Second Carnatic War's complexity stems from simultaneous succession disputes in two regions — Carnatic and Hyderabad — each with competing European-backed claimants.

• Option (a): Incorrectly matched. Muzaffar Jung was the French-backed claimant to the Hyderabad succession, supported by Dupleix — not the English-backed candidate.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched. Nasir Jung was supported by the English in the Hyderabad succession — pairing him with French backing reverses the actual alignment.
• Option (c): Correctly matched. Muhammad Ali was the English East India Company's supported claimant to the Carnatic Nawabship. After the death of his father Anwaruddin at the Battle of Ambur (1749), Muhammad Ali continued the resistance against the French-backed Chanda Sahib from Trichinopoly. His security was the object of Clive's Arcot operation.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched. Anwaruddin was the incumbent Nawab before the Second Carnatic War fully opened — he was killed at Ambur (1749). His son Muhammad Ali, not Anwaruddin himself, became the English-backed claimant going forward.

Value Addition:
• Memory aid: French backed the challengers (Chanda Sahib, Muzaffar Jung); English backed the incumbents/defenders (Muhammad Ali, Nasir Jung).
• Muhammad Ali remained Nawab of Carnatic under English protection until the late 18th century — a textbook example of a pliant dependent ally.
• Battle of Ambur (1749), where Anwaruddin was killed, is the opening military engagement of the Second Carnatic War.
